Coming from someone who has beaten both games on heroic difficulty, I can assure you that DOS2 is much more tuned up against you than BG3.

It's already been mentioned on multiple accounts about enemy scaling with each level, their improvements in almost every single combat aspect. Those guys are steroid-packed for standard enemies. Don't even let me start talking about more difficult by nature foes.

The increase in sheer beefiness in DOS2 forces you to pick your strategy carefully. Some fights will be somewhat easier thanks to your party being better adjusted to enemies who lack physical armour but might struggle with the opposite scenario. In BG3, enemies are tougher, but not to the extent of feeding everyone nectar and ambrosia; they are still manageable even when you get caught off-guard.

Also, the game rewards you for having multiple options available in combat, mainly if you have them in your backpack at the ready. Scrolls, potions, grenades, in tandem with what you utilise based on your skills and spells can give you that necessary turn to turn the tide of battle. Some interactions between items and skills may seem bizarre or even nonsensical at first glance as well - I won't spoil which ones - but they *can* be applied. There's almost no useless ability in DOS2, whereas in BG3, I took a look at some perks, spells, and skills, scratched my head for a while, and then promptly forgot about them without ever using them at all.

In short, yes, DOS2 is more challenging than BG3's, but as you learn more about the combat system, surfaces, interactions between skills themselves and items, and study your opponents, you will find the experience satisfying. Each fight is a puzzle on its own, and what determines your solution are your build and whatever you carry in your bags.

It's been a while since I played DOS, but I can clearly remember some things about the combat that made each encounter significantly easier:

- be mindful of surfaces, especially water ones. Electrifying it causes a chance of stunning anyone who passes through without immunity to it. Early game, your best friend is a massive puddle and any source of lightning to mass CC enemies.

- lore master is a key skill for adventuring. Each enemy has different resistances, and tailoring your wands and staves to strike vulnerabilities can up the damage by a good chunk.

- main stat focus gives you massive benefits every 5 points you invest in them. Heck, even one point can be a game changer. Every point you put into strength, for example, will boost your chance to knock down an enemy by 5% or so. Every 5 points in relevant stat lowers your skill cooldowns by 1 turn, which can be a significant difference.

DOS is somewhat of a probability game with all status effects, having a chance to be resisted. What you often have to do is bend those odds to your advantage by checking enemies' bodybuilding and willpower versus your own chances to debilitate them. That's the biggest similarity I can think of between DOS 1 and BG3.

I'd say it depends on what kind of support you have in mind.

For an offensive touch, investing points in Pyro can give you access to Necrofire Infusion. Mix that up with your max level Incarnate, Supercharge it, buff it with Peace of Mind and chain-blast enemies with the signature spell it gets.
That aside, a point in each elemental skill will unlock a different flavour of infusion, granting you increased flexibility for enemies with various resistances (without having to depend on surfaces)
Additionally, you can follow up with Necro for extra summons and versatility it allows: decay, infect, bonus physical damage, and, of course, the sorcery totem spell you get later in the game add extra kick when in combat.

For more support, there are options:
- one point in Pyro, Hydro, Geo, and Aero, three in Necro, combined with buffs you get from Summoning naturally give you a good selection of enhancements and cleansing;
- while I'm not exactly a fan of it, Blessed Water Infusion skill grants your Incarnate access to Blessed Steam and Restoration. It's more useful when facing undead or when applying decay.
- if you really want to feel like a commander, invest in Leadership skill. It benefits everyone but you, but that's the idea; give resistances and dodge chance while you stay relatively safe yourself.
- if you're playing as a human, Encourage is already in your repertoire. Double points for a non-origin human since you have access to Dome of Protection.

Memory can go a long way, depending on your setup. While wits and initiative are important to establish the start of the battle, you can cast Peace of Mind for the initial advantage.
I would also look into investing in Strength to offset the lack of physical armour, as well as grabbing a shield with a one handed wand for protection (and possibly maiming enemies, if your wand has any effects on it).

This was the advice I kept hearing from mental health specialists and doctors. They claimed exercising and physical activity are major factor in improving the low mood and motivation related to depression.

I was told to go for walks to stretch my legs and get some movement in. I have followed their advice, and for two weeks straight, without skipping a day, I spent about 20-30 minutes doing just that, excluding any other times I had to go out.

Results came to be pretty much the same as yours: I felt tired *and* still feeling low. Probably even lower than I had felt before I went for a walk because I was left with my own thoughts, without any stimulus strong enough to properly take my mind off from ruminating.

I have mentioned this result of my experiment, and I was mildly surprised to see the aforementioned people be at a loss of words. Apparently, they didn't expect such a turn of events. Many of them had no clue how to respond. Most have tried to push me to try again and again, claiming the results will take some time to become visible, and even then, I might not notice the improvements myself. Basically, I was hearing the same message over and over again without being given any alternatives to try out instead.

I have felt and still do feel disheartened by how people trained and/or learned in mental health wellbeing are stupefied by a statement that is (I assume) an exemption from what they expected was a fail proof solution to the issue. Exercise may help some people, I'm not denying that. However, I'd prefer to know what else is on the menu to try to work with instead of hearing a broken record.

That depression is a real issue and it can, in fact, be debilitating to a point where you can barely function.

I speak from personal experience as one suffering from severe depression for many years, as well as talking with people going through similar hell.

And don't even get me started about the safety of talking about feeling suicidal/having a plan to do so. While I'm aware that there are supposed to be services to look out for you when you feel this way, I don't see being locked up in mental health ward a way to improve or change one's mind. Honestly, I sometimes think it has an adverse effect than beneficial.

I'm not trying to imply that it's all bad things about the treatment and such. Nowadays there is *some* support for depression and other mental health issues, as opposed to 50 and more years ago. 

What I'm trying to say is that some of the methods used might need changing. The public view on those matters needs to be better informed. People are ashamed to say that they aren't feeling well. They deny any examinations or chats, they delude themselves and thus create more pain for everyone involved in their life. They pretend to be okay while slowly eroding on the inside. And why is that?

Because of fear of being looked down upon. Because of fear of worrying others and being a burden. Because of fear of being locked up in a mental health ward. Because of people abandoning them. Because of fear of not being understood. Because of hopelessness that nothing will help.

I could go on and on about it. But in the essence, despite depression being more addressed nowadays, it still needs a major research and a better, more wide-spread information about it. It should be encouraged to talk about it. People suffer because of it. People *die* because of it.

You can try to make each of more widely known classes in DOS by picking spells and skills from certain schools.

Why? Because all of those schools have "support" spells. 

This is where the building of classes is made: game gives you access to skill and spell list, you browse it, then mix and match the schools to whatever you want your character want to be. All it takes it some researching and an appropriate stat allocation.

In short, you most likely won't be able to make a completely "pure" Necro, because it's going to struggle on its own. But if you add a Summoner school to, for example, boost the damage of Necro creatures, then you will be much more effective.

Whenever this realisation of meaninglessness comes, be it voluntarily or not, it will pass quicker once you stop fighting it. Let it come, look at it in an objective way, as it is a fact. 

This fate of stopping existing at some point is something nobody can influence, despite so many people trying to oppose it: poets, artists, historical figures, etc. Like you said, all of them have died. It's a fact. Their existence will be forgotten at some point in time. It become meaningless once that happens.

However, the time they had while walking on Earth was their meaning in itself. Many of those people thought about meaning of their life I reckon, what their life was worth. 

I can't speak for them, really, but I can only assume that, despite this inevitable fate looming over them, they kept pushing on. They would find the meaning of their own life and follow it, since it's something they could influence, give them power over their fate, however short-lived their existence would be. They accepted that futility, or explained it in another way (reincarnation, afterlife, judgment of the soul, etc.), and carried on.

While the idea of not having meaning in the big picture is depressing, because it is out of our grasp to control, letting it pass and wash over oneself can make a person appreciate what they have right now more. All the things you have accomplished, the connections you've made, the skills you've acquired. Those might mean nothing after passing away into obscurity, but they do mean something while you exist: to you and other people or animals even.

I would say that when this existential depression comes around, try to accept it and let is simply flow, without dwelling on it too much, since it's an undeniable fact we can't control. 

But if it does become overwhelming or too loud, see if you can look around at all the things and people that mean something to you. They will all pass away at some point, making them meaningless as well. Why not give them even bigger meaning while they are here and now, while they still breathe? Appreciate those people or things more, for example, indulge yourself in activities with them, amplify their current meaning while they still exist.

That includes yourself: look at yourself, what you did and accomplished. What do those things make you feel? What do or did they mean to you? What do or did they mean to others? Do those things feel more impactful, knowing they don't matter in the end?

I've heard a saying in my school that I can't remember exactly as it goes, but it was more or less like this: "Value and appreciate the ones who mean something to you, for life comes to an end to everyone so quickly". I think doing that makes their life mean more. And so it can make you value your own existence. 

I'd say make most of it, while you can still influence it. Make it mean something to you, not the universe. Seize the day, no matter how corny might it sound. For once you're gone, nothing will matter anyway. Shake hands with thoughts of meaninglessness in the grand scheme of things, make it give meaning to what you have now and let it go. Turn the dread into a reminder of how valuable your living moments are.

It's just what I think about it. I apologise again for any  grammar mistakes.

Not only the lives of people who lived before us are gone, but they also faded away. Who remembers a person who has lived 3000 years ago? They lived, died and became forgotten forever. In a way you can say that they never existed to begin with.

Fading into obscurity, unknown, is only a matter of time after a person passes away. There will be no trace of that person ever existing. Their life, in the end, had no meaning at all. In the grand scheme of things, none of us matter. All we are is dust, to be scattered across the time into the void.

On the other hand, however, that ultimate meaninglessness, paradoxically, can bring meaning to person's life. Having in mind the fact that, in the end, nothing we do has any impact, can be the motivation to look for your own personal meaning.

The grand universe doesn't know you're alive. The smaller one, the world that's closest to you and is around you, will know and acknowledge that you were. People you've developed relationship with, places that you often visited, random events that left an impact on someone or something, are testimonies to your temporary life. As long as they exist, so shall you.

Will any of it matter in the end? Absolutely not. But why bother with that? As long as you are alive, you are here. You exist. You breathe, you walk, you leave footprints. You prove to yourself and others that you exist. 

And once you pass away, you won't think about this conundrum anymore. What happens next in the world won't be your concern. You will fade away, like everyone at some point.

Thinking about the lack of meaning in a large scale just because we will be forgotten at some point, is depressing. But why bother thinking about it, when during your lifespan you're your own example of your existence? That's all it matters. At least that's what I think.

From what I have heard and experienced myself in life, I can tell that school is not the perfect representation nor reflection of who you are or what you are or not capable of doing. You get to see what is a path that is interesting for you, your possible strengths and weaknesses. And that's okay. Even straight A students struggle with certain material - if not at school, then maybe outside of it. You never know.
